source_text: Sed omittamus sane testimonia prophetarum, ne minus idonea probatio uideatur esse de his quibus omnino non creditur. ueniamus ad auctores et eos ipsos ad ueri probationem testes citemus, quibus contra nos uti solent, poetas dico ac philosophos. ex his unum deum probemus necesse est, non quod illi habuerint cognitam ueritatem, sed quod ueritatis ipsius tanta uis est, ut nemo possit esse tam caecus, quin uideat ingerentem se oculis diuinam claritatem. poetae igitur quamuis deos carminibus ornauerint et eorum res gestas amplificauerint summis laudibus, saepissime tamen confitentur spiritu uel mente una contineri regique omnia. Orpheus, qui est uetustissimus poetarum et aequalis ipsorum deorum, siquidem traditur inter Argonautas cum Tyndaridis et Hercule nauigasse, deum uerum et magnum πρωτόγονον appellat, quod ante ipsum nihil sit genitum, sed ab ipso sint cuncta generata. eundem etiam Φάνητα nominat, quod cum adhuc nihil esset, primus ex infinito apparuerit et extiterit. cuius onginem atque naturam quia concipere animo non poterat, ex aere inmenso natum esse dixit: πρωτόγονος Φαέθων περιμήϰεος ἠέρος υἱός. aliut enim amplius quod diceret non habebat. hunc ait esse omnium deorum parentem, quorum causa caelum condiderit liberisque prospexerit, ut haberent habitaculum sedemque communem: ἔϰτισεν ἀθανάτοις δόμον άϕθιτον. natura igitur et ratione ducente intellexit esse praestantissimam potestatem, caeli ac terrae conditricem. non poterat enim dicere Iouem esse principem rerum, qui erat Saturno genitus, neque ipsum Saturnum, qui caelo natus ferebatur; caelum autem tamquam deum primum constituere non audebat, quod uidebat elementum esse mundi, quod ipsum eguerit auctore. haec eum ratio perduxit ad deum illum primogenitum, cui adsignat et tribuit principatum. Homerus nihil nobis dare potuit quod pertineat ad ueritatem: qui humana potius quam diuina conscripsit. potuit Hesiodus, qui deorum generationem unius libri opere conplexus est: sed tamen nihil dedit non a deo conditore sumens exordium, sed a chao, quod est rudis inordinataeque materiae confusa congeries, cum explanare ante debuerit chaos ipsum unde quando quomodo esse aut constare coepisset. nimirum sicut ab aliquo artifice disposita ordinata effecta sunt omnia, sic ipsam materiam fictam esse ab aliquo necesse est. quis igitur hanc nisi deus fecit, cuius potestati subiacent omnia? sed refugit hoc ille, dum horret incognitam ueritatem. non enim Musarum instinctu sicut uideri uolebat in Helicone carmen illut effudit, sed meditatus uenerat ac paratus. nostrorum primus Maro non longe afuit a ueritate, cuius de summo deo, quem mentem ac spiritum nominauit, haec uerba sunt: principio caelum ac terras camposque liquentis lucentemque globum lunae Titaniaque astra spiritus intus alit totamque infusa per artus mens agitat molem et magno se corpore miscet. ac ne quis forte ignoraret, quisnam esset ille spiritus qui tantum haberet potestatis, declarauit alio loco dicens: deum namque ire per omnis terrasque tractusque maris caelumque profundum; hinc pecudes armenta uiros genus omne ferarum, quemque sibi tenuis nascentem accersere uitas. Ouidius quoque in principio praeclari operis sine ulla nominis dissimulatione a deo, quem fabricatorem mundi, quem rerum opificem uocat, mundum fatetur instructum. quodsi uel Orpheus uel hi nostri quae natura ducente senserunt in perpetuum defendissent, eandem quam nos sequimur doctrinam conprehensa ueritate tenuissent. Sed hactenus de poetis. ad philosophos ueniamus, quorum grauior est auctoritas certiusque iudicium, quia noti rebus commenticiis, sed inuestigandae ueritati studuisse creduntur. Thales Milesius, qui unus e septem sapientium numero fuit quique primus omnium quaesisse de causis naturalibus traditur, aquam esse dixit ex qua nata sint omnia, deum autem esse mentem quae ex aqua cuncta formauerit. ita materiam rerum posuit in umore, principium causamque nascendi constituit in deo. Pythagoras ita definiuit quid esset deus: animus per uniuersas mundi partes omnemque naturam commeans atque diffusus, ex quo omnia quae nascuntur animalia uitam capiunt. Anaxagoras deum esse dicit infinitam mentem quae per se ipsam moueatur: Antisthenes multos quidem esse populares deos, unum tamen naturalem id est summae totius artificem. Cleanthes et Anaximenes aethera esse dicunt summum deum, cui opinioni poeta noster adsensit: tum pater omnipotens fecundis imbribus aether coniugis in gremium laetae descendit et omnis magnus alit magno permixtus corpore fetus. Chrysippus naturalem uim diuina ratione praeditam, interdum diuinam necessitatem deum nuncupat, item Zenon naturalem diuinamque legem. horum omnium sententia quamuis sit incerta, eodem tamen spectat, ut prouidentiam unam esse consentiant. siue enim natura siue aether siue ratio siue mens siue fatalis necessitas siue diuina lex siue quid aliut dixeris, idem est quod a nobis dicitur deus. nec obstat appellationum diuersitas, cum ipsa significatione ad unum omnia reuoluantur. Anstoteles quamuis secum lpse dissideat ac repugnantia sibi et dicat et sentiat, in summum tamen unam mentem mundo praeesse testatur. Plato, qui omnium sapientissimus iudicatur, monarchian plane aperteque defendit nec aethera aut rationem aut naturam, sed ut est deum nominat: ah eo mundum hunc perfectum atque mirabilem esse fabricatum. quem Cicero secutus atque imitatus in plurimis frequenter deum confitetur ac supremum uocat in iis libris quos de legibus scripsit; ab eoque regi mundum argumentatur, cum disputat de natura deorum, hoc modo: nihil est praestantius deo. ab eo igitur mundum regi necesse est. nulli igitur est naturae oboediens aut subiectus deus. omnem ergo regit ipse naturam. quia autem sit deus, m uonsoiatione dehmt: nec uero deus ipse, qui intellegitur a nobis, alio modo intellegi potest nisi mens soluta quaedam et libera, segregata ab omni concretione mortali, omnia sentiens I et mouens. Annaeus quoque Seneca, qui ex Romanis uel acerrimus Stoicus fuit, quam saepe summum deum merita. laude prosequitur! nam cum de inmatura morte dissereret, non intellegis inquit auctoritatem ac maiestatem iudicis tui, rectoris orbis terrarum caelique et deorum omnium dei, a quo ista numina quae singula adoramus et colimus suspensa sunt? item in Exhortationibus: hic cum prima fundamenta molis pulcherrimae iaceret et hoc ordiretur quo neque maius quicquam nouit natura nec melius, ut omnia sub ducibus suis irent, quamuis ipse per totum se corpus intenderat, tamen ministros regni sui deus genuit. et quam multa alia de deo nostris similia locutus est! quae nunc differo, quod aliis locis opportuniora sunt. nunc satis est demonstrare summo ingenio uiros attigisse ueritatem ac paene tenuisse, nisi eos retrorsus infucata prauis opinionibus consuetudo rapuisset, qua et deos esse alios opinabantur et ea quae in usum hominis deus fecit, tamquam sensu praedita essent, pro diis habenda et colenda credebant.
thought_title: Proof of One God from Pagan Authors
pass_a_gloss: But let us omit the testimonies of the prophets, lest the proof seem less suitable for those things which are not believed at all. Let us come to the authors and cite them as witnesses to the proof of the truth, those whom they are accustomed to use against us, I say the poets and philosophers. From these, we must prove one God, not because they had known the truth, but because the power of truth itself is so great that no one can be so blind that he does not see the divine clarity being forced upon his eyes. Therefore, the poets, although they have adorned the gods with songs and amplified their deeds with the highest praises, nevertheless very often confess that all things are contained and ruled by one spirit or mind. Orpheus, who is the most ancient of the poets and a contemporary of the gods themselves, since he is said to have sailed among the Argonauts with Tyndaridis and Hercules, calls the true and great God 'protogonos', because nothing was generated before him, but all things were generated from him. He also names him 'Phaneta', because when nothing else existed, he first appeared and existed from the infinite. Because he could not conceive his origin and nature in his mind, he said that he was born from the immense air: 'Protogonos Phaethon, son of vast air'. For he had nothing else to say. He says that this God is the parent of all the gods, for whose sake he founded the heaven and provided for his children, so that they might have a common dwelling and seat: 'He created a house for the immortals'. Therefore, led by nature and reason, he understood that there is a most excellent power, the creator of heaven and earth. For he could not say that Jupiter was the principle of things, who was born from Saturn, nor Saturn himself, who was said to be born from heaven; but he did not dare to establish heaven as the first god, because he saw that it was an element of the world, which itself needed an author. This reason led him to that primary God, to whom he assigns and attributes the principle. Homer could not give us anything that pertains to the truth: for he wrote human rather than divine things. Hesiod could have, who encompassed the generation of the gods in one book: but nevertheless, he did not give anything, not taking the beginning from the God who created, but from chaos, which is a confused mass of raw and disordered matter, when he ought to have explained chaos itself, whence, when, and how it began to exist. For just as all things were disposed, ordered, and made by some craftsman, so it is necessary that this matter itself was made by someone. Who, therefore, made it, if not God, to whose power all things are subject? But he shuns this, while he shudders at the unknown truth. For he did not pour out that song on Helicon, as he wished to seem, by the instinct of the Muses, but he came meditated and prepared. Our first poet, Maro, was not far from the truth, who said these words about the highest God, whom he named mind and spirit: 'In the beginning, the spirit nourishes the heaven and the earth and the fields and the shining globe of the moon and the Titania stars, and the mind, infused through all the parts, moves the mass and mixes with the great body'. And lest anyone might be ignorant of who this spirit is, who has so much power, he declared in another place, saying: 'For God goes through all the lands and the tracts of the sea and the deep heaven; from him, the flocks and herds and men and every kind of wild beast, and every nascent life is summoned'. Ovid also, at the beginning of his renowned work, without any dissimulation of the name, confesses that the world was instructed by God, whom he calls the maker of the world, the craftsman of things. If Orpheus or our poets, led by nature, had defended what they perceived in perpetuity, they would have held the same doctrine, having grasped the truth. But so much for the poets. Let us come to the philosophers, whose authority is weightier and judgment more certain, because they are believed to have studied not fictional things, but to investigate the truth. Thales of Miletus, who was one of the seven sages and who is said to have been the first to seek the natural causes, said that water is the source from which all things were born, and that God is the mind which formed all things from water. Thus, he placed the matter of things in moisture, and established the principle and cause of birth in God. Pythagoras defined what God is: 'The mind that goes through all parts of the world and all nature, and is diffused, from which all living things take life'. Anaxagoras says that God is an infinite mind that moves by itself: Antisthenes says that there are many popular gods, but one natural God, that is, the craftsman of the whole. Cleanthes and Anaximenes say that the highest God is the ether, to which opinion our poet assented: 'Then the omnipotent Father, with fertile rains, descends into the bosom of his joyful consort, and nourishes all the great offspring, mixed with the great body'. Chrysippus calls the natural power, endowed with divine reason, sometimes divine necessity, God; likewise, Zenon calls the natural and divine law God. The opinion of all these, although it is uncertain, nevertheless looks to the same thing, that they agree there is one providence. For whether you say nature, or ether, or reason, or mind, or fatal necessity, or divine law, or anything else, it is the same as what we say is God. Nor does the diversity of names hinder, since all things are reduced to one signification. Aristotle, although he disagrees with himself and says and thinks contradictory things, nevertheless testifies that one mind presides over the world. Plato, who is judged the wisest of all, plainly and openly defends the monarchy, and does not name the ether, or reason, or nature, but calls him God: 'From him, this world was made perfect and wonderful'. Which Cicero, following and imitating in many things, frequently confesses and calls the supreme God in the books he wrote on the laws; and argues that the world is ruled by him, when he disputes about the nature of the gods, in this way: 'Nothing is more excellent than God. Therefore, it is necessary that the world is ruled by him. For God is not subject to any nature, nor is he obedient to it. Therefore, he rules all nature himself'. Because, however, he is God, I omit the association of him: nor can God himself, who is understood by us, be understood in any other way than as a certain mind, free and separated from all mortal concretion, perceiving and moving all things. Annaeus Seneca, who was one of the most keen Stoics among the Romans, how often does he pursue the supreme God with deserved praise! For when he was discussing premature death, he says: 'Do you not understand the authority and majesty of your judge, the ruler of the earth and heaven and all the gods, from whom those divinities which we adore and worship individually are suspended?' Likewise, in his Exhortations: 'When he laid the first foundations of this most beautiful work and began to arrange it, so that all things might go under their leaders, although he himself had extended throughout his whole body, nevertheless, God generated the ministers of his kingdom'. And how many other things did he say about God, similar to ours! Which I now defer, because they are more opportune in other places. Now it is enough to demonstrate that men of the highest genius have touched the truth and almost grasped it, unless they were drawn back by the customary, perverse opinions, by which they believed that there are other gods, and that the things which God made for the use of men are to be held and worshiped as gods.
pass_b_english: Let us set aside the testimony of the prophets, lest the proof seem less fitting for matters that are not believed at all. Instead, let us turn to the authors whom our opponents customarily cite against us—the poets and philosophers—and call them as witnesses to the truth. From these sources we must demonstrate one God, not because they possessed a full knowledge of the truth, but because the power of truth itself is so great that no one can be so blind as to miss the divine clarity forced upon his eyes. The poets, although they adorned the gods with songs and magnified their deeds with the highest praise, nevertheless confess again and again that all things are contained and governed by a single spirit or mind. Orpheus, the most ancient of the poets and a contemporary of the gods themselves—since tradition says he sailed with the Argonauts alongside Castor and Hercules—calls the true and great God 'Protogonos,' because nothing was generated before him, but all things were generated from him. He also names him 'Phaneta,' because when nothing else yet existed, he first appeared and stood forth from the infinite. Since he could not grasp this God's origin and nature in his mind, he declared that he was born from the vast air: 'Protogonos Phaethon, son of boundless air.' He had nothing further to say. Orpheus calls this God the parent of all the gods, for whose sake he founded the heavens and provided for his children, so that they might share a common dwelling and seat: 'He established an imperishable home for the immortals.' Guided by nature and reason, he therefore understood that a supreme power exists, the creator of heaven and earth. He could not say that Jupiter was the first principle, since Jupiter was born of Saturn, nor Saturn himself, who was said to be born of heaven; yet he dared not make heaven the first god, because he saw that heaven is an element of the world, and an element needs an author. Reason thus led him to that primal God, to whom he assigns and attributes sovereignty. Homer can give us nothing that pertains to the truth, for he wrote of human rather than divine matters. Hesiod might have, since he encompassed the genealogy of the gods in a single work; yet he contributed nothing, because he took his starting point not from the Creator God but from Chaos, a confused mass of raw and disordered matter, when he ought first to have explained whence, when, and how Chaos itself began to exist. Just as all things are ordered and fashioned by some craftsman, so this matter itself must have been made by someone. Who made it, if not God, to whose power all things are subject? But Hesiod shrinks from this, shuddering at the unknown truth. That song on Helicon was not poured out by the instinct of the Muses, as he wished to appear; he came to it after meditation and preparation. Our own first poet, Vergil, was not far from the truth. Speaking of the highest God, whom he named Mind and Spirit, he wrote: 'In the beginning the spirit nourishes heaven and earth and the fields and the shining globe of the moon and the Titans' stars; and the mind, infused through every part, moves the whole mass and mingles with the great body.' And lest anyone be ignorant of who this spirit is that wields such power, Vergil declared elsewhere: 'For God goes through all lands and the tracts of the sea and the deep heaven; from him come the flocks and herds and men and every kind of wild beast, and every nascent life is summoned.' Ovid also, at the start of his renowned work, confesses without disguise that the world was ordered by God, whom he calls the world's maker and the craftsman of things. If Orpheus or our poets, led by nature, had defended forever what they perceived, they would have held the same doctrine we follow, having grasped the truth. So much for the poets. Let us turn to the philosophers, whose authority is weightier and judgment more certain, because they are believed to have studied not fictions but the investigation of truth. Thales of Miletus, one of the Seven Sages and the first to seek natural causes, said that water is the source from which all things are born, and that God is the mind which formed all things from water. Thus he placed the material of things in moisture, and established the principle and cause of generation in God. Pythagoras defined God as: the mind that pervades all parts of the world and all nature, diffused throughout, from which all living creatures receive life. Anaxagoras says God is an infinite mind that moves itself. Antisthenes allows many popular gods, but one natural God—that is, the craftsman of the whole. Cleanthes and Anaximenes call the highest God the ether, an opinion our poet Vergil endorsed: 'Then the omnipotent Father, with fertile rains, descends into the bosom of his joyful consort, and nourishes all the great offspring, mixed with the great body.' Chrysippus names the natural power endowed with divine reason—sometimes calling it divine necessity—God; likewise, Zeno calls the natural and divine law God. The opinions of all these, though uncertain, nevertheless converge on the same point: they agree that there is one providence. Whether you call it nature, ether, reason, mind, fatal necessity, divine law, or anything else, it is the same as what we call God. Nor does the diversity of names obstruct this, since all are reduced to a single signification by their very meaning. Aristotle, although he contradicts himself and says and thinks opposing things, nevertheless testifies that one mind presides over the world. Plato, judged the wisest of all, defends the monarchy plainly and openly; he does not name the ether, or reason, or nature, but calls him God: 'From him this world was made perfect and wonderful.' Cicero, following and imitating Plato in many respects, frequently confesses and calls the supreme God in the books he wrote on the laws, and argues that the world is ruled by him when he disputes the nature of the gods: 'Nothing is more excellent than God. Therefore the world must be ruled by him. For God is not subject to any nature, nor obedient to it. Therefore he himself rules all nature.' Because he is God, I pass over the question of his association; nor can God himself, as we understand him, be understood in any other way than as a mind that is free and released, set apart from all mortal concretion, perceiving and moving all things. Annaeus Seneca, the keenest Stoic among the Romans, how often does he extol the supreme God with deserved praise! When discussing premature death he says: 'Do you not understand the authority and majesty of your judge, the ruler of earth and heaven and all the gods, from whom those divinities which we individually adore and worship are suspended?' Likewise in his Exhortations: 'When he laid the first foundations of this most beautiful structure and began to arrange it so that all things might proceed under their leaders, although he himself had extended through his whole body, nevertheless God generated the ministers of his kingdom.' And how many other things he said about God, similar to our own! I defer those now, because they are more opportune in other places. For the present it is enough to show that men of the highest genius have touched the truth and almost grasped it, unless they were dragged back by the entrenched custom of perverse opinions—opinions by which they believed there are other gods, and that the things God made for human use are to be revered and worshiped as gods.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text, including the nuances of the philosophical arguments and the specific poetic quotations. All citations (e.g., Orpheus, Maro, Ovid, Thales, Pythagoras, etc.) are correctly handled. The translation of 'Tyndaridis' as 'Castor' in Pass B is a valid identification of the mythological figure (Castor and Pollux), and 'Maro' as 'Vergil' is the standard identification. The translation of 'm uonsoiatione dehmt' (likely an OCR error for 'm uonsoiatione deum' or similar) is handled by the translator's decision to omit/pass over the association, which aligns with the sense of the surrounding text.

The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the meaning, structure, and key terms. The citations to Orpheus, Homer, Hesiod, and other philosophers are correctly rendered, and the theological arguments are maintained. The title 'Proof of One God from Pagan Authors' appropriately captures the content of the passage.
